Working notes:
- Recent demand is variable but typically 4–8 units/day (observed: 8, 5, 4, 8, 1, 4, 4, 5, 4); plan around ~5/day rather than relying on low outliers.
- Stockouts are expensive (1.00 per lost unit), while holding costs are low (~0.10/unit) and ordering costs are ~0.50/order. Favor adequate safety stock and avoid running inventory to zero.
- Replenishment appears to take 1–2 days. Include both on-hand stock and expected arrivals when calculating inventory position, but retain coverage for demand during the lead time.
- A practical target is roughly 10–15 units of inventory position (about two to three days of typical demand), increasing orders when projected available stock falls below that. Order enough to restore the target, not automatically a fixed quantity.
- Do not skip an order solely because stock is currently zero if incoming units are already committed; check whether arrivals cover lead-time demand and the next day afterward. Day 9’s zero order left only 1 unit on hand and led to a day-10 stockout.
- Recent repeated small orders (4–5) were insufficient when demand was 8 and arrivals lagged, causing costly stockouts on days 5–10. Prefer a somewhat larger order before/through high-demand periods.
- Operational notes (forklift certification, receiving temp, shifted carrier pickup) may increase delivery risk or timing uncertainty; carry extra buffer when they affect receiving.

Working notes:
- Demand is variable and has recently run higher: commonly 5–6 units/day, with spikes of 8–10. Plan around 6/day and allow for 10-unit days rather than using low outliers.
- Stockouts are very expensive (1.00 per lost unit); holding costs are low (~0.10/unit) and ordering costs are ~0.50/order. Favor a meaningful buffer.
- Replenishment takes roughly 1–2 days, but receiving/pickup disruptions (new temps, forklift certification, shifted carrier pickup) increase timing risk. Treat arrivals as potentially delayed when such notes apply.
- Inventory position should include on-hand plus committed arrivals, but zero on-hand is dangerous even when arrivals are scheduled. Retain enough stock for current demand, lead-time demand, and at least one day afterward.
- Raise the practical target from 10–15 to roughly 15–20 units of inventory position during unstable/high-demand periods (about 2–3 days of demand). Order to restore the target, not a fixed quantity.
- Recent experience confirms that repeated 5–10-unit orders were insufficient while starting from zero: days 11 and 16–19 lost 5–8 units each despite incoming stock. Larger orders and earlier replenishment are warranted.
- Never skip an order merely because arrivals are committed or current stock is zero. Day 20’s zero order caused another 6-unit stockout, even with 10 units arriving on each of the next two days.
- When on hand is zero and demand is running 5–10/day, order enough to cover the immediate day plus expected lead-time demand—often 10–15 units or more—while checking all scheduled arrivals and their timing.
- Counts have recently matched the system; no adjustment is currently needed.

Working notes:
- Demand is variable and has shifted high: typically 5–6 units/day, often 8–13, with occasional zero. Plan around 8–10/day during recent high-demand periods; do not rely on low outliers.
- Stockouts cost 1.00/unit, versus ~0.10/unit holding and ~0.50/order. Bias toward adequate buffer and earlier replenishment.
- Lead time is roughly 1–2 days, but receiving, forklift, racking, counting, and carrier changes can delay or disrupt arrivals. Treat scheduled receipts as uncertain, especially with an ops note.
- Inventory position includes on-hand plus committed arrivals, but committed stock cannot reliably cover today’s demand. Always protect immediate demand with on-hand or an order; zero on-hand is dangerous even with receipts due.
- During unstable/high-demand periods, target at least 15–20 units, and consider 20–25 when on hand is low or arrival timing is risky. This represents roughly 2–3 days of demand plus a buffer.
- Order to restore the target, not a fixed quantity. Do not skip orders merely because receipts are scheduled.
- If on hand is zero with demand around 8–13/day, order at least 15–20 units (more if receipts are delayed or demand is elevated), while checking receipt timing. Recent 10–15-unit orders still produced large stockouts when starting empty.
- When on hand is only a few units, order before depletion even if arrivals are committed. A zero order was safe only when on hand plus reliable near-term receipts covered demand; otherwise it caused avoidable risk.
- Recent outcomes: 15–20-unit orders with timely receipts prevented stockouts on days 23–25 and 28–30; 7–15-unit orders while empty or exposed led to losses. Favor larger, earlier orders over repeated small orders.
- Counts have matched the system; no adjustment currently needed.

Working notes:
- Demand is variable, recently averaging roughly 5–10/day with spikes to 13–14 and occasional zero. Use ~8–10/day for planning, but do not overreact to one-day spikes or zeros.
- Stockout costs 1.00/unit versus ~0.10/unit holding and ~0.50/order. Avoid stockouts, but excess inventory creates substantial holding cost; do not build a large buffer when on-hand stock already covers several days.
- Lead time is roughly 1–2 days, but receiving, forklift, racking, counting, carrier, and staffing changes can delay or disrupt arrivals. Treat receipts as helpful but uncertain, especially with an ops note.
- Inventory position includes on-hand plus committed arrivals, but committed stock should not be relied on to cover today’s demand when on-hand is very low. Protect immediate demand with on-hand or an order.
- In unstable/high-demand periods, target about 15–20 units, potentially 20–25 when on hand is near zero and receipts are risky. When on hand is 25–40 units, normally do not order unless demand or receipt risk clearly warrants it.
- Order to restore a reasonable target, not a fixed quantity. Favor earlier/larger orders when exposed, but avoid repeated small orders or ordering merely because stock is declining.
- If on hand is zero or only a few units with demand around 8–13/day, order at least 15–20 units and verify receipt timing. Recent 20-unit orders from low stock prevented stockouts.
- Recent experience: 20-unit orders on days 31–32 avoided stockouts; subsequent zero orders while on hand rose to 26–40 were appropriate, though holding costs were high. A 10-unit order at 28 on hand was unnecessary but did not cause a stockout.
- Counts have matched the system; no adjustment currently needed.
